title: Op-art paper dress
lede: A disposable dress of bonded-fibre paper from the Scott Paper Company, printed all over with a black and white op-art check.
summary: A sleeveless shift printed edge to edge with a distorted black and white checkerboard. Scott Paper Company, USA, 1966.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.30-1992 (1200 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: The black and white op check moved straight onto a cheap mass-market garment: an all-over field of squares that compress and expand.

context: The V&A catalogues the dress with the style “Op art” and describes “a repeating black and white op art printed pattern” on bonded fibre paper. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O147891/).

The V&A says Scott Paper Company invented the paper dress in 1966 as a marketing tool: for one dollar a buyer got the dress and coupons for Scott paper products, and the company received about half a million orders in under a year. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O147891/).
A later promotional paper dress with a Pop print is [the Campbell’s “Souper” dress](ref:campbells-souper-paper-dress-1967).
observed: A sleeveless A-line shift with a round neck and two patch pockets, photographed flat on black.
The whole surface carries one black and white print: checkerboard bands in which the squares change size, alternating with rows of small open squares inside larger ones.
Where fine checks meet coarse checks, the rows seem to bend and bulge.
The print runs across the seams and pockets without matching them. A plain white band finishes the hem.
interpretation: The dress applies the op rule of one unit changed by steps: the square is the only motif, and only its size and grouping change.
As a throwaway paper product, it shows how quickly the gallery look of 1965 became a mass-market print.
borrow: Build a pattern from one square unit whose size changes by steps across bands.
Let an all-over pattern run through seams, pockets, or panel edges, so that the field reads as continuous.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is not openly licensed, and the rights in the print are unverified.
